Tents never touch, not even at a corner. When you place a tent, the cells around it are grass: no tent can go there.
Start with the rows and columns that have a 0: they are all grass. Then find a tree that has only one free cell left next to it; its tent must be there.
A queen shuts its row, its column and both diagonals. When a row has only one free cell left, the queen goes there.
Start from the locked queens. Cross out everything they reach, then look for a row or column with a single cell left.
Shaded cells never touch each other. So when you shade a cell, the cells right next to it stay: they are safe.
A number that is alone in its row and its column is safe, never shade it. Only numbers that appear twice can be shaded: pick one of each pair.
When half of a line is one digit, the rest is the other digit. This column has two 0s, so the last cell is 1. This one has two 1s, so the last cell is 0.
Find two equal digits side by side. A 0 0 gets a 1 next to it, and once a line has two 0s the rest of it are 1s. Here the row 0 0 ends with 1 1.
A lamp lights its row and column until a wall stops it. No other lamp may stand in that light, so those cells get a cross.
Look at the numbers on the walls first. A wall that says 2 and has only two free cells beside it needs a lamp on both.
The sign points its tip at the smaller number. Next to a 2 the bigger cell has to be 3, so the 3 goes in the cell the sign opens toward.
Find a row or column that has all but one number. The last cell is the number that is missing: 2 and 1 are here, so the last one is 3.
When a square has as many lines as its number says, its other sides get no line. This 3 has three sides, so the fourth is marked with a cross.
Start with a 3 in a corner. The corner point can only have both its lines or none, and none would leave only two sides, so both outer sides are drawn.
Every cell belongs to one rectangle with one number. This 2 cannot use the cell on its left, it is taken, or the 4 below it, so it takes the free cell on its right.
Look at a big number in a corner. A 1 by 4 or 4 by 1 shape would run over other numbers, so the 4 in the corner can only be a 2 by 2.
A line that adds up to more than its target is too big by the difference. 4 + 7 + 2 is 13 and the target is 6, so erase the number that is 7.
Start with a line whose sum is already its target: nothing is erased there. 3 + 9 + 5 is 17, so keep all three. The same goes for the first column.
An arrow with another arrow in front of its head cannot leave. Take the arrow in the way out first, then the ones waiting behind it are free.
Start with an arrow that has nothing in front of its head. This one points right and the way is clear, so it leaves at once.
No pipe may point out of the board. If a pipe on the edge has an end pointing out, turn it until its ends look at neighbors.
Start with the corners. A bent pipe in a corner fits only one way, with both of its ends inside the board. Turn it until it does.
A shape is a group too. The row, the column and the shape of this cell show eight of the nine digits, so the missing digit goes here.
Look for the shape that is already almost full. When only a cell or two is left in it, the missing digits go there. It is the easiest place to start.
A tap flips the light you touch and the ones beside it. Here a tap on the corner puts out all three lit lights at once.
Start at the top row. Tap the cell right under a lit light in the top row and it goes out. Keep going down row by row.
Finish the top row first, then the left column. Do not touch tiles that are in place, so you never undo them.
The easiest start: bring tile 1 to the top left corner, then line up 2 and 3 beside it.
To move a big disk, first put the ones on top of it on the third tower. With 3 disks, move the small two to the middle, then the big one goes to the empty goal.
With an odd number of disks (3, 5) move the smallest disk to the goal tower, with an even number (4, 6) to the middle tower. That is the first move.
A block slides only along its own line: a flat block left and right, a tall block up and down. Slide the tall block that is in the way down, and the orange block leaves.
Look at the way out of the orange block. Find the block that stands in it and play that one first.
Leave a finished tube alone. Put two half tubes of one colour together: one tube fills, one empties, and an empty tube is useful.
Use the empty tube: put the top colour in it to free the colour buried below. Then pour that colour onto its own colour.
Build a product that is a little over the target and take the extra away. 6 x 5 = 30, the target is 28: 30 - 2 = 28.
Start with the product that comes nearest to the target. 3 x 4 = 12 is close to 14, then add the 2 that is left.
The ball keeps sliding in one direction and only stops at a wall or the edge. Every cell it passes is painted.
Look at all four ways the ball can go and start with the one that paints the most cells.
A dot with the dots of other colours round it has one way to go. The blue dot has other colours on its left and below, so its path goes right.
Start with a dot that is hemmed in. The yellow dot at the bottom has other colours on its left and above, so its path goes right: drag from there.
Take a stick from one digit and add it to another: that stick closes the difference between the two sides. When you hold a stick, the places it can go show.
Work out both sides of the equation first and find the difference. Look for the digit to take a stick from and the digit to add it to so that the difference closes.
A beam that meets a mirror turns a right angle. The beam going left to right turns up at this mirror and lights the target.
Think back from the target. Which line must the beam come along? Put a mirror where that line meets the path of the beam.
Move one end of two crossing lines to a free place where it crosses nothing. The lines turn green.
Pick one of the red lines and drag the point at its end to a place where its lines cross nothing. Corners are often a good place.
Keep the green letters where they are. Yellow letters are in the word but elsewhere: try them in other boxes. Do not use a grey letter again.
For the first try pick a word full of common letters, especially vowels. The colours show at once which letters are in the word.
Remember where the cards that did not match are. When you later see the same shape somewhere else, open its pair at once: a pair in two moves.
In the first rounds always open new cards: a shape you have not seen is worth more than a lucky match. Once cards are familiar, pairs are easy.
Remember the squares as one shape, not one by one: an L, a line, a corner. A shape is easy to recall.
In the first round one square lights up, which is easy. Keep your eyes in the middle of the grid and the place is easy to recall.
Leave a word that fits more than one group for last. Find the sure groups first, and the four words left are the last group.
Start with the narrowest topic, such as planets or colours. Before picking four words make sure they all truly fit the same topic.
Carry each value you find into the next rows: if three bananas make 6, a banana is 2, and a banana times an apple is 6, so an apple is 3. The last row is 3 + 2 + 2 = 7.
Start with the row that has only one kind of fruit. If three bananas make 6, each is worth 2.
Keep the colour with a solid green ring where it is. Try the dashed green colours in other places and never use a grey colour again.
For the first try use four different colours: the rings show at once which colours are in the code.
A corner square that is not the start or the end has the line through both of its neighbours. Draw the lines of these two corners first.
Start at 1 and move on without leaving a square behind or a dead end. Pass the numbers in order: you cannot reach 3 without 2.
Paint this cell. Its mirror image, the ringed cell across the axis, is painted.
Empty this cell. The ringed cell across the axis is empty.
Paint the mirror image of the ready half so both sides match
The line splits the board in two. One half is ready. Paint the other half so it is the mirror image of it.
Tap a cell in the empty half to paint it. Tap again to empty it. The ready half never changes.
Every cell is the same as the cell the same distance from the line on the other side. If that one is painted, paint this one; if it is empty, leave it.

The axis is not always vertical. On a horizontal axis the top half is ready, on a diagonal the cells above it, and around the middle point the board is turned half a way round. Find the cell across, then copy it.
Start with the painted cells of the ready half. Each one gives a cell to paint across the axis. Begin with the ones closest to it so you do not lose your place.
These two numbers follow the same rule: %1$s. The odd one is another number.
Four numbers follow a rule and one does not. Find the one that does not
Five numbers, pick the one that breaks the rule
breaks the rule, the right answer
wrong pick, it follows the rule
Four of the five numbers follow a hidden rule and one does not. Tap the number that does not.
A right pick turns green, the rule is shown and the next round comes. One wrong pick ends the run.
Look at even and odd first. If four are even, look for the odd one, and the other way round. Then check for multiples of 5.
If four numbers fit two rules, try a third. These numbers are all odd, but four of them are multiples of 3.
Put the numbers in order of size. When you look for the rule that joins four of them, start with the smallest and the biggest.
Put %1$d here: it is the last empty cell of its block, and this digit completes the sum.
Put %1$d here: the sum of its block and the digits in it allow no other digit.
Put %1$d here: it is the only digit both of its blocks allow.
This digit is not right. Tap the same digit to take it out.
Write 1-9: no repeats in a block, sums must match
Cross sums board, %1$d by %2$d, %3$d of %4$d cells filled
Take out the digits you put
Write the digits 1 to 9 in the empty cells. The number in a dark cell is the sum of the row next to it or the column below it.
Tap a cell first, then a key below to pick the digit. Tap the same key again and the cell is emptied.
A digit cannot be used twice in a block. When a rule breaks, the cells of that block turn red.
Some sums have only one way. In three cells 7 is only 1, 2 and 4. The other block says which digit goes in which cell.
The last empty cell of a block gets the digit that completes the sum. With a sum of 17 and 9 and 7 already in it, the last cell is 1.
Find the block with the fewest choices: the smallest or the biggest sums. Start with sums like 7 in three cells; the digits you find open the blocks beside them too.
The sequence plays again. Watch it and touch the same order.
Your turn: touch them in the same order
That was not the next one
Start the run over with a new sequence
Press start, then remember the lit buttons
The lights are hidden now. Find the order, watch again with a hint, or start over
Coloured buttons light up one after the other, each with its own note. Keep the order in mind.
When the lights stop, touch the same buttons in the same order. It works with the sound off too: every button has its own colour and shape.
Every round the sequence gets one step longer. One wrong button ends the run, and the rounds you cleared are your result.
Group the buttons in threes: three lights are easy to hold as one piece. Keep the rhythm of the notes too, the sounds help you recall the order.
In the first round only one button lights up. After you press start, give the screen your eyes and ears and find the button that lit.
Rule this cube out: two of its faces are opposite faces of the net, so they are never seen together. They are the ringed squares of the net.
Rule this cube out: the three faces are right but they turn the wrong way round. Follow the ringed squares of the net as it folds.
Which cube does the net fold to? Tap it
Right! The net folds to this cube
This cube shows two opposite faces together, which a folded cube never does
The three faces are right but turn the wrong way round, a folded cube never looks like this
The net does not fold to that cube
You see an unfolded cube, a net. Every square has its own symbol. Which cube do you get when the net is folded?
You look at the cube from a corner and see three faces: the top one, the left one and the right one. Find those three faces on the net.
Tap the cube the net folds to. A wrong cube ends the run, a right one brings a new net.
Opposite faces are never seen together. In a straight row of the net, two squares with one square between them are opposite. Rule out a cube that shows both.
Even when the three faces are right, the turning order matters. Follow the three squares as you fold the net: a cube with the order reversed cannot come from this net.
First find the opposite pairs. Then rule out the cubes that show two opposite faces. In the ones left, check the turning order of the faces.
Shortest time first, then the fewest moves. Puzzles you won without help count.
Most rounds cleared first, then the shortest time. Runs you played without help count.
Fewest guesses first, then the shortest time. Puzzles you won without help count.
Most stars first, then the shortest time. The daily puzzle counts.
